docs.title: Turbo Docs
docs.text:
Turbo is a distributed residential proxy network. Traffic enters through a self-hosted proxy server (SOCKS5 / HTTP CONNECT) and exits through residential client nodes over TLS-encrypted QUIC.

Choose the section that matches your role:

Audience What you’ll find For Businesses How to authenticate, target countries/sessions, and integrate SOCKS5 or HTTP with ready-made code templates For Infrastructure How to deploy the stack, configure services, and understand architecture and infra choices

docs.title: Quick start (buyers)
docs.text:
curl -x "socks5h://country=US:YOUR_API_KEY@PROXY_HOST:1080" https://httpbin.org/ip

See Authentication & targeting and Code templates for more.

docs.title: Quick start (operators)
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/L1shed/Turbo.git
cd Turbo
docker compose up --build

See Setup & deployment for prerequisites and environment variables.

docs.title: Need access?
docs.text:
Bandwidth purchases are currently arranged via:

  • Telegram
  • Discord (DM from the maintainer’s GitHub profile)

docs.title: For Businesses
docs.text: Use Turbo as a residential proxy endpoint for scraping, account workflows, or any HTTPS traffic that needs high-quality exit IPs.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• SOCKS5 on port 1080 (primary interface)
  • HTTP CONNECT on port 8081 (HTTPS tunneling)
  • Username-based targeting — country, sticky sessions, residential hints
  • API key as password — credits are looked up in Redis

docs.title: Integration path
docs.text:
1. Obtain an API key (credits) from the network operator
  2. Configure authentication & targeting
  3. Connect via SOCKS5 or HTTP
  4. Copy a code template for your stack

docs.title: Connection string shape
docs.text:
protocol://USERNAME:API_KEY@HOST:PORT
Part Meaning USERNAME Targeting parameters (not a login name), e.g. country=US,sessionId=abc API_KEY Your credential / password HOST Proxy server hostname PORT 1080 (SOCKS5) or 8081 (HTTP)

docs.title: Supported request types
docs.text: Protocol Supported Notes SOCKS5 CONNECT Yes IPv4, IPv6, and domain names HTTP CONNECT (HTTPS) Yes Tunnel only Plain HTTP proxy No Non-CONNECT requests are rejected by default

docs.title: Authentication & targeting
docs.text:
Turbo uses username/password auth on both SOCKS5 and HTTP.

  • Password = your API key (looked up against Redis credits)
  • Username = a comma-separated list of targeting parameters

Tip

There is no anonymous access. Clients must send credentials on every connection.

docs.title: Username parameters
docs.text: Parameter Example Effect country country=US Route via a node in that ISO-3166-1 alpha-2 country Country shorthand US Same as country=US when the token is a valid 2-letter code sessionId / sess* sessionId=abc123 Sticky session identifier (any key containing sess) Residential hint resid_ip or any token containing resi Marks the request as residential group

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
country=US
country=DE,sessionId=checkout-42
resid_ip,US
country=GB,sessid=sticky-1

Full proxy URLs:

socks5h://country=US:YOUR_API_KEY@proxy.example.com:1080
socks5h://country=DE,sessionId=abc123:YOUR_API_KEY@proxy.example.com:1080
socks5h://resid_ip,US:YOUR_API_KEY@proxy.example.com:1080

URL encoding

Commas and = in the username are fine in most libraries when passed as discrete username/password fields. If you embed them in a URL string, URL-encode special characters when required by your client.

docs.title: Password (API key)
docs.text: The password is your API key. The proxy validates it against the credits store. Failed lookups reject the connection (unless the server is running with DEBUG_MODE=1 for local development).

docs.title: Country codes
docs.text:
Country values must be valid ISO-3166-1 alpha-2 codes (US, DE, FR, …). Invalid codes are ignored and traffic falls back to the global node pool.

If no country is specified, the balancer selects from the global pool.

docs.title: Sticky sessions
docs.text:
Pass any parameter whose key contains sess (for example sessionId, sessid, sess). The value is available for session-aware routing on the server side.

country=US,sessionId=user-checkout-001

Reuse the same sessionId across requests when you need the same residential exit characteristics for a workflow.

docs.title: HTTP proxy
docs.text: Turbo exposes an HTTP CONNECT proxy for HTTPS tunneling. The conventional listen port is 8081.

docs.title: Endpoint
docs.text:
Setting Value Protocol HTTP proxy (CONNECT) Port 8081 Auth Proxy-Authorization: Basic Methods CONNECT only

HTTPS only by default

Non-CONNECT requests (plain HTTP proxying) are rejected. Use CONNECT for https:// destinations.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Same model as SOCKS5:

  • Username = targeting parameters (country=US, …)
  • Password = API key

Sent as HTTP Basic auth in the Proxy-Authorization header.

docs.title: Quick test
docs.text: curl -x "http://country=US:YOUR_API_KEY@PROXY_HOST:8081" https://httpbin.org/ip

docs.title: How CONNECT works
docs.text:
1. Client sends CONNECT host:443 HTTP/1.1 with Basic proxy auth
  2. Server authenticates and selects a residential node
  3. Server responds 200 Connection Established
  4. Client performs TLS (or any TCP protocol) through the tunnel
  5. Bytes are relayed via the node to the destination

docs.title: When to use HTTP vs SOCKS5
docs.text:
Use case Prefer General-purpose clients, scrapers, libraries with SOCKS support SOCKS5 Tools that only speak HTTP CONNECT HTTP on 8081 Need remote DNS resolution SOCKS5 with socks5h://

Both share the same auth and targeting parameters.

docs.title: SOCKS5 proxy
docs.text: SOCKS5 is the primary buyer interface. The server listens on TCP port 1080.

docs.title: Endpoint
docs.text:
Setting Value Protocol SOCKS5 Port 1080 Auth Username / password (method 0x02) Commands CONNECT only

Prefer socks5h:// (hostname resolved by the proxy) over socks5:// when your client supports it, so DNS happens on the residential exit path.

docs.title: Quick test
docs.text: curl -x "socks5h://country=US:YOUR_API_KEY@PROXY_HOST:1080" https://httpbin.org/ip

docs.title: Auth handshake (overview)
docs.text:
1. Client offers username/password authentication
  2. Username is parsed as targeting parameters
  3. Password is validated as the API key
  4. Client sends CONNECT with the destination host and port
  5. Server picks a node (by country or global), opens the path over QUIC, and relays bytes bidirectionally

docs.title: Destination formats
docs.text:
SOCKS5 destinations may be:

  • IPv4 address
  • IPv6 address
  • Fully qualified domain name (FQDN)

docs.title: Retries & availability
docs.text: If no suitable node answers in time, the server may retry with another node (up to a few attempts). If the pool for the requested country is empty, you get a connection failure — try global (omit country) or another region.

docs.title: Browser / system proxy
docs.text:
Point your SOCKS5-capable client at:

Host: PROXY_HOST
Port: 1080
Username: country=US
Password: YOUR_API_KEY

Not all browsers support SOCKS username/password natively; use an extension, a local forwarder, or an HTTP CONNECT client instead.

docs.title: Code templates
docs.text:
Copy-paste examples for connecting through Turbo. Replace:

Placeholder Value PROXY_HOST Your proxy hostname YOUR_API_KEY Your API key (password) Username Targeting string, e.g. country=US

docs.title: Protocols
docs.text:
• SOCKS5 — port 1080 — preferred when available
  • HTTP CONNECT — port 8081 — for HTTPS tunnels

docs.title: HTTP CONNECT with HttpClient
docs.text:
using System.Net;
using System.Net.Http.Headers;

var proxy = new WebProxy("http://PROXY_HOST:8081")
{
    Credentials = new NetworkCredential("country=US", "YOUR_API_KEY")
};

var handler = new HttpClientHandler
{
    Proxy = proxy,
    UseProxy = true
};

using var client = new HttpClient(handler);
client.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);

var response = await client.GetStringAsync("https://httpbin.org/ip");
Console.WriteLine(response);

docs.title: SOCKS5 (.NET 6+)
docs.text:
using System.Net;

var handler = new SocketsHttpHandler
{
    ConnectCallback = async (context, cancellationToken) =>
    {
        // Prefer a SOCKS5 library that supports username/password,
        // e.g. PipeSocks / custom CONNECT via MihaZupan.HttpToSocks5Proxy
        throw new NotImplementedException(
            "Use a SOCKS5 auth-capable library, or HTTP CONNECT on port 8081."
        );
    }
};

Practical option — MihaZupan.HttpToSocks5Proxy or similar:

// Install-Package MihaZupan.HttpToSocks5Proxy

var proxy = new HttpToSocks5Proxy(
    "PROXY_HOST",
    1080,
    "country=US",
    "YOUR_API_KEY"
);

var handler = new HttpClientHandler { Proxy = proxy };
using var client = new HttpClient(handler);

var ip = await client.GetStringAsync("https://httpbin.org/ip");
Console.WriteLine(ip);

docs.title: Go
docs.text: go get golang.org/x/net/proxy

docs.title: SOCKS5 with net/http
docs.text:
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "time"

    "golang.org/x/net/proxy"
)

func main() {
    dialer, err := proxy.SOCKS5(
        "tcp",
        "PROXY_HOST:1080",
        &proxy.Auth{
            User:     "country=US",
            Password: "YOUR_API_KEY",
        },
        proxy.Direct,
    )
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    client := &http.Client{
        Transport: &http.Transport{
            Dial: dialer.Dial,
        },
        Timeout: 30 * time.Second,
    }

    resp, err := client.Get("https://httpbin.org/ip")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

docs.title: HTTP CONNECT
docs.text:
package main

import (
    "encoding/base64"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    proxyURL, err := url.Parse("http://PROXY_HOST:8081")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    transport := &http.Transport{
        Proxy: http.ProxyURL(proxyURL),
        ProxyConnectHeader: http.Header{
            "Proxy-Authorization": []string{
                "Basic " + basicAuth("country=US", "YOUR_API_KEY"),
            },
        },
    }

    client := &http.Client{Transport: transport, Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
    resp, err := client.Get("https://httpbin.org/ip")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

func basicAuth(user, pass string) string {
    return base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString([]byte(user + ":" + pass))
}

Tip

Embedding credentials in the proxy URL also works for many Go HTTP clients:

http://country=US:YOUR_API_KEY@PROXY_HOST:8081

docs.title: Java
docs.text: Example using OkHttp with a SOCKS proxy. Auth for SOCKS username/password requires a custom Authenticator on the JVM, or an HTTP CONNECT proxy instead.

docs.title: HTTP CONNECT with OkHttp
docs.text:
import okhttp3.Credentials;
import okhttp3.OkHttpClient;
import okhttp3.Request;
import okhttp3.Response;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.net.InetSocketAddress;
import java.net.Proxy;

public class TurboHttpExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Proxy proxy = new Proxy(
            Proxy.Type.HTTP,
            new InetSocketAddress("PROXY_HOST", 8081)
        );

        String credential = Credentials.basic("country=US", "YOUR_API_KEY");

        OkHttpClient client = new OkHttpClient.Builder()
            .proxy(proxy)
            .proxyAuthenticator((route, response) ->
                response.request().newBuilder()
                    .header("Proxy-Authorization", credential)
                    .build()
            )
            .build();

        Request request = new Request.Builder()
            .url("https://httpbin.org/ip")
            .build();

        try (Response response = client.newCall(request).execute()) {
            System.out.println(response.body().string());
        }
    }
}

docs.title: SOCKS5 (system properties)
docs.text:
For libraries that honor JVM SOCKS settings without username support, prefer HTTP CONNECT above, or use a library that supports SOCKS5 auth (for example Netty or Apache HttpClient 5 with a SOCKS tunnel).

Minimal SOCKS without auth (only works if the server allows it — Turbo does not):

// Not sufficient for Turbo — credentials are required.
System.setProperty("socksProxyHost", "PROXY_HOST");
System.setProperty("socksProxyPort", "1080");

docs.title: fetch + socks-proxy-agent (SOCKS5)
docs.text:
import { SocksProxyAgent } from "socks-proxy-agent";

const agent = new SocksProxyAgent(
  "socks5h://country=US:YOUR_API_KEY@PROXY_HOST:1080"
);

const res = await fetch("https://httpbin.org/ip", { agent });
console.log(await res.json());

Note

Native fetch in Node 18+ may expect dispatcher (undici) rather than agent. Prefer axios or node-fetch if agent is ignored.

docs.title: Sticky session helper
docs.text:
function turboSocks({ host, apiKey, country = "US", sessionId }) {
  let user = `country=${country}`;
  if (sessionId) user += `,sessionId=${sessionId}`;
  return `socks5h://${user}:${apiKey}@${host}:1080`;
}

const agent = new SocksProxyAgent(
  turboSocks({
    host: "PROXY_HOST",
    apiKey: "YOUR_API_KEY",
    country: "DE",
    sessionId: "checkout-1",
  })
);

docs.title: aiohttp + aiohttp-socks
docs.text:
import asyncio
import aiohttp
from aiohttp_socks import ProxyConnector

async def main():
    connector = ProxyConnector.from_url(
        "socks5h://country=US:YOUR_API_KEY@PROXY_HOST:1080"
    )
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession(connector=connector) as session:
        async with session.get("https://httpbin.org/ip") as resp:
            print(await resp.json())

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Sticky session helper
docs.text:
def turbo_proxy(country: str, api_key: str, host: str, session_id: str | None = None) -> str:
    user = f"country={country}"
    if session_id:
        user += f",sessionId={session_id}"
    return f"socks5h://{user}:{api_key}@{host}:1080"

proxies = {
    "http": turbo_proxy("US", "YOUR_API_KEY", "PROXY_HOST", "scrape-1"),
    "https": turbo_proxy("US", "YOUR_API_KEY", "PROXY_HOST", "scrape-1"),
}

docs.title: For Infrastructure
docs.text: This section is for operators and developers who deploy, configure, or extend the Turbo proxy server and its surrounding stack.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Topic Page System components & traffic flow Architecture Docker Compose & first boot Setup & deployment Environment variables & ports Configuration Why QUIC, Redis, ClickHouse, … Design choices Metrics, Grafana, stats UI Observability Client nodes & pairing Running nodes

docs.title: Stack at a glance
docs.text:
Buyers ──SOCKS5 :1080 / HTTP :8081──► Proxy Server ──QUIC :8443/udp──► Residential Nodes
                                            │
                         Redis · Supabase · ClickHouse · Prometheus/Grafana

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Docker and Docker Compose
  • A Supabase (or compatible Postgres) DATABASE_URL for node registry / pairing
  • Optional: Discord bot token, production TLS for QUIC beyond the built-in self-signed cert

Start with Setup & deployment.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Turbo separates buyers (proxy clients), the proxy server, and residential nodes.

docs.title: Global view
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    User(Buyer / scraper)
    subgraph SelfHosted [Self-hosted backend]
        ProxyServer[Proxy Server]
        Redis[(Redis — auth & streams)]
        AI[AI traffic analysis]
    end
    ClientNode[Client Node]
    NodeRunner(Node operator)
    PaymentGateway[Payment Gateway]
    Blockchain[(Crypto)]
    TargetWebsite[Target Website]
    Website[Next.js Website]
    Supabase[(Supabase PostgreSQL)]

    User -->|SOCKS5 / HTTP CONNECT| ProxyServer
    User -->|Buys credits| PaymentGateway

    ProxyServer -->|Node updates| Supabase
    ProxyServer <-->|TLS QUIC| ClientNode
    ProxyServer -->|Auth & credits| Redis

    AI -->|Evaluates connections| Redis

    ClientNode -->|TCP egress| TargetWebsite
    NodeRunner -->|Operates| ClientNode

    PaymentGateway -->|Payments| Blockchain
    PaymentGateway -->|Credits| Redis

    Blockchain -->|Rewards| NodeRunner
    Website -->|Dashboard / pairing| NodeRunner
    Supabase <-->|Realtime| Website

docs.title: Traffic flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Buyer
    participant Server as Proxy Server
    participant Node as Client Node
    participant Net as Internet

    Buyer->>Server: 1. SOCKS5 / HTTP CONNECT
    Server->>Node: 2. Dest + payload over QUIC
    Node->>Net: 3. TCP to target
    Net-->>Node: 4. Response
    Node-->>Server: 5. QUIC data
    Server-->>Buyer: 6. Relay back

docs.title: Process responsibilities
docs.text: Component Role Proxy server (this repo) Accept buyer connections, authenticate, select nodes, relay over QUIC, expose metrics/stats Redis API-key credits, pub/sub / streams for connection features Supabase Postgres Node registry, pairing requests, activity flags ClickHouse Session feature analytics (session_features) Client node (separate binary) Egress TCP from residential IP; pairs via website Website (separate Next.js app) Operator dashboard and node pairing UX Prometheus / Grafana Scraping and dashboards

docs.title: Ports (server)
docs.text: Port Protocol Purpose 1080 TCP SOCKS5 for buyers 8081 TCP HTTP CONNECT for buyers 8080 TCP /metrics (Prometheus), /stats (HTML) 8443 UDP QUIC to client nodes

docs.title: Node selection
docs.text: Connected nodes are grouped into country pools (and a global pool). Selection is weighted by node score (latency + reliability). Buyers request a country via the SOCKS/HTTP username; if none is set, the global pool is used.

docs.title: QUIC messaging
docs.text:
Nodes and the server exchange newline-delimited JSON messages on a bidirectional QUIC stream (ALPN turbo-proxy), including:

Type Direction Purpose connect server → node Open a user tunnel to addr with optional first payload data both Base64 payload for an active connection ID close both Tear down a user connection ping / pong both Health / latency measurement address node → server Crypto payout address pairing_url server → node Pairing link for unpaired nodes

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Variable Required Default Purpose DATABASE_URL Yes — Supabase / Postgres DSN for nodes and pairing REDIS_ADDR No localhost:6379 Redis host:port CLICKHOUSE_ADDR No localhost:9000 ClickHouse native protocol CLICKHOUSE_DATABASE No default Database name CLICKHOUSE_USER No default User CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD No empty Password DEBUG_MODE No unset When 1, auth succeeds even if Redis credit lookup fails DISCORD_TOKEN No unset If set, starts the Discord bot

ClickHouse init failure is logged as a warning; Supabase init failure is fatal.

docs.title: Listener ports
docs.text:
Configured in code / Compose port mappings:

Port Mapping in Compose Service 1080 1080:1080 SOCKS5 (started in main) 8081 8081:8081 HTTP CONNECT (HTTPProxy implemented; ensure a listener is started in main for production) 8080 8080:8080 Prometheus /metrics, HTML /stats 8443/udp 8443:8443/udp QUIC nodes

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
Used for:

  • Buyer API-key → credits lookup
  • Streams / pub-sub for connection features (AI pipeline)

Compose enables AOF persistence under .logs/redis-data.

docs.title: Supabase / Postgres
docs.text:
Stores:

  • Connected node metadata and activity
  • Pairing requests (node_connect_requests) claimed by the website

The website (separate repo) consumes the same project via realtime.

docs.title: ClickHouse
docs.text: Stores session-level features for analytics and future anomaly detection. Migrations live under clickhouse/migrations/ and run via the migrate Compose service.

docs.title: TLS / QUIC
docs.text:
At startup the server generates a self-signed certificate and listens with:

  • InsecureSkipVerify: true (dev-oriented)
  • ALPN protocol name: turbo-proxy

For production, inject a proper certificate and tighten verification on the node client.

docs.title: Design choices
docs.text: Why the Turbo server is shaped the way it is.

docs.title: QUIC for node transport
docs.text:
Choice: Nodes connect to the server over QUIC (UDP 8443) with TLS and ALPN turbo-proxy, not long-lived TCP or WebSockets.

Rationale:

  • Multiplexed streams without head-of-line blocking at the transport layer
  • Built-in TLS encryption suitable for untrusted residential networks
  • Better behavior on unstable / NAT-heavy residential links than raw TCP tunnels
  • Single bidirectional stream carries newline-delimited JSON control + data messages

Implementation uses quic-go.

docs.title: SOCKS5 (+ HTTP CONNECT) for buyers
docs.text:
Choice: Buyers speak industry-standard SOCKS5 and HTTP CONNECT.

Rationale:

  • Works with existing scrapers, browsers, and language libraries
  • Username field doubles as a compact targeting DSL (country=US,sessionId=…)
  • Password maps cleanly to API keys / credits

SOCKS5 is started in main; HTTP CONNECT is implemented for the same auth and routing model.

docs.title: Redis for credentials
docs.text:
Choice: Credits live in Redis, not only in Postgres.

Rationale:

  • Low-latency auth on every buyer connection
  • Fits payment gateway updates and future pub/sub for AI / abuse signals
  • Streams can carry connection feature events without coupling to the request path

docs.title: Supabase for nodes & pairing
docs.text:
Choice: Node registry and pairing use Supabase Postgres (+ realtime for the website).

Rationale:

  • Relational model for nodes, activity, and connect requests
  • Website can subscribe to pairing / node state without the Go server owning the UX
  • Operators can manage data with familiar SQL tooling

docs.title: ClickHouse for session analytics
docs.text:
Choice: High-volume session features go to ClickHouse.

Rationale:

  • Columnar storage suited to ML / anomaly features over many connections
  • Keeps hot auth path (Redis) and OLTP (Supabase) free of analytical load
  • Optional: server continues if ClickHouse is unavailable

docs.title: Weighted country pools
docs.text:
Choice: Nodes are scored (latency + reliability) and selected with weighted random draws inside country (or global) pools.

Rationale:

  • Prefer healthier exits without hard-sticking to a single node
  • Country targeting for buyers without a full BGP / geo-IP product on the server
  • Geo for new nodes is enriched via a public IP API at connect time

docs.title: Self-hosted commercial core
docs.text:
Choice: Apache 2.0 server you can run yourself; client and website live in separate repos.

Rationale:

  • Operators can white-label monetization (payments, rewards, pricing)
  • Clear boundary: this repository is the control plane + buyer edge
  • Nodes remain downloadable binaries paired through the web app

docs.title: Observability stack
docs.text:
Choice: Prometheus + Grafana (+ Redis exporter) shipped in Compose.

Rationale:

  • Standard metrics endpoint on :8080/metrics
  • Ops teams can reuse existing Prom/Grafana workflows
  • /stats provides a lightweight HTML view for quick node inspection

docs.title: Running nodes
docs.text: Client nodes share residential bandwidth and connect to your proxy server over QUIC. The node binary and website live outside this server repository; pairing still depends on Supabase rows created by the server.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: Platform Supported Windows Yes macOS Yes Linux Yes Mobile No

docs.title: Install (network operators / earners)
docs.text:
1. Download the latest release for your platform
  2. Run the executable — a tray icon appears
  3. Choose Connect to pair with an account
  4. Complete auth in the browser; the node appears on the dashboard

You can run multiple nodes on distinct networks / IPs.

docs.title: Pairing flow
docs.text:
1. Unpaired node opens a QUIC session to the server
  2. Server creates a pairing request and sends a pairing_url
  3. Operator opens the URL (hosted website), authenticates, and claims the node
  4. Node is associated with their account and can earn rewards

Self-hosters must point nodes at their server’s QUIC endpoint and use a website / Supabase project wired to the same DATABASE_URL.

docs.title: Scoring
docs.text:
Node score combines:

  • Latency (L) — typically clamped (e.g. 10ms–500ms range in product docs)
  • Reliability (R)

$$ S = w_L \cdot L + w_R \cdot R $$

Product documentation weights latency at 40% and reliability at 60%. Higher scores increase selection weight in the balancer pools.

docs.title: Monetization (public network)
docs.text: On the public Turbo network, base reward is about $0.10 / GB, with bonuses for streaks and long-lived stable connections. Self-hosters define their own payment and reward logic.

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text: Nodes must reach the server on UDP 8443 (QUIC). Buyers do not connect to nodes directly.

docs.title: Built-in HTTP endpoints
docs.text:
The proxy serves on :8080:

Path Description /metrics Prometheus metrics /stats HTML dashboard of connected nodes /stats?address=<crypto> Filter stats by node payout address 
curl -s http://localhost:8080/metrics | head
open http://localhost:8080/stats

docs.title: Prometheus
docs.text:
Compose runs Prometheus with config under metrics/prometheus.yml and alert rules in metrics/alert_rules.yml.

  • UI: http://localhost:9090
  • Ensure scrape targets point at the backend service name and port 8080

docs.title: Grafana
docs.text:
• UI: http://localhost:3000
  • Default admin password in Compose: proxy199 (change in production)
  • Provisioning under metrics/grafana/provisioning/
  • Worldmap plugin installed via Compose for geo-oriented panels

docs.title: Redis exporter
docs.text: Exposes Redis metrics on :9121 for Prometheus scraping.

docs.title: What to watch
docs.text: Signal Why Active QUIC clients Capacity / coverage Auth failures Bad keys or Redis outages Node scores / ping latency Exit quality ClickHouse insert errors Analytics pipeline health Country pool emptiness Targeting failures for buyers

docs.title: Local development tip
docs.text: With few or no paired nodes, buyer requests fail at node selection even if auth succeeds. Pair at least one client node before load-testing scrapers.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Docker Engine and Docker Compose v2
  • Git
  • A Postgres connection string for Supabase (or compatible), exposed as DATABASE_URL

docs.title: Clone and run
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/L1shed/Turbo.git
cd Turbo
docker compose up --build

This starts:

Service Description backend Go proxy server redis Auth / credits / streams clickhouse + migrate Analytics DB and schema migrations prometheus Metrics scrape grafana Dashboards (default admin password proxy199) redis-exporter Redis metrics for Prometheus

docs.title: Required environment
docs.text:
Compose sets REDIS_ADDR=redis:6379 for the backend. You must also provide:

export DATABASE_URL="postgresql://..."

Pass it into the backend service (compose environment / .env file). Without it, the server exits on startup.

Optional:

export DEBUG_MODE=1          # skip Redis credit failures (local only)
export DISCORD_TOKEN=...     # enable Discord bot
export CLICKHOUSE_ADDR=...   # if not using defaults

See Configuration for the full list.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
# SOCKS5 (needs a valid API key in Redis, or DEBUG_MODE=1)
curl -x "socks5h://country=US:test@localhost:1080" https://example.com

# Stats UI
open http://localhost:8080/stats

# Prometheus metrics
curl -s http://localhost:8080/metrics | head

docs.title: Build without Compose
docs.text:
# Requires local Redis, ClickHouse (optional), and DATABASE_URL
go build -o server .
REDIS_ADDR=localhost:6379 DATABASE_URL=... ./server

The multi-stage Dockerfile builds a static Alpine image running ./server.

docs.title: Production notes
docs.text:
• Put buyer ports (1080, 8081) and QUIC (8443/udp) behind a firewall / allowlist as needed
  • Replace the runtime self-signed QUIC certificate for production node trust
  • Persist Redis (appendonly) and ClickHouse volumes
  • Provision Grafana secrets instead of the compose default password
  • Ensure Prometheus scrape targets match the Compose service name (backend vs legacy app)
